::: {.paper-ref}
**Dimitris Bertsimas and Melvyn Sim** (2004). "The Price of Robustness."
*Operations Research* 52(1), 35–53.
[doi:10.1287/opre.1030.0065](https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.1030.0065) [@bertsimas2004]
:::

## Context

By the early 2000s there were two main ways to make a linear program robust to errors in its
coefficients.

- @soyster1973 required each constraint to hold when *all* uncertain coefficients take
  their worst values together. The result is again an LP, but it is very conservative.
- Ben-Tal and Nemirovski [-@bental1998; -@bental1999; -@bental2000] and El Ghaoui and
  coauthors [-@elghaoui1997; -@elghaoui1998] used
  ellipsoidal uncertainty sets. These are far less conservative and come with probability
  guarantees, but the robust counterpart is a second-order cone program. That is harder to
  solve at scale and, more importantly, awkward when some variables are integer.

The paper asks whether one can have both: the linearity of Soyster's approach and the
moderate conservatism of the ellipsoidal one. The title names the quantity to be kept small:
the objective value given up to gain protection.

## Main contributions

**1. A budget of uncertainty per constraint.** Each row $i$ gets a parameter
$\Gamma_i \in [0, \lvert J_i\rvert]$, where $J_i$ is the set of its uncertain coefficients.
The solution must stay feasible when any $\lfloor\Gamma_i\rfloor$ of them take their worst
values and one more moves part of the way. $\Gamma_i = 0$ is the nominal model and
$\Gamma_i = \lvert J_i\rvert$ is Soyster's; values in between tune the conservatism of each
row separately. See [The Model](../budget-of-uncertainty.qmd#the-model).

**2. The robust counterpart is an LP (or a MIP).** The worst case over subsets is written as
a small LP (Proposition 1) and replaced by its dual, which turns the robust problem into one
linear program (Theorem 1). It adds a threshold variable per row and one variable per
uncertain coefficient, keeps the sparsity of the constraint matrix, and keeps integer
variables integer. This is what makes the approach usable for discrete optimization. See
[From a max inside a constraint to an LP](../budget-of-uncertainty.qmd#from-a-max-inside-a-constraint-to-an-lp).

**3. Probability bounds that do not depend on the solution.** If the deviations are
independent, symmetric and bounded, a robust solution violates row $i$ with probability at
most $e^{-\Gamma_i^2/(2\lvert J_i\rvert)}$ (Theorem 2), and at most a sharper binomial bound
$B(\lvert J_i\rvert, \Gamma_i)$ that is tight for $\pm 1$ deviations (Theorem 3). Since
$B(n, \Gamma) \approx 1 - \Phi((\Gamma - 1)/\sqrt n)$, a budget of order $\sqrt n$ already
gives a small violation probability. See
[How likely is a violation?](../budget-of-uncertainty.qmd#how-likely-is-a-violation).

**4. Extensions.** The paper compares the conservatism of the budget and ellipsoidal sets
(Section 4.1), gives the derivative of the optimal value with respect to $\Gamma_i$
(Theorem 4), and extends the model and the bounds to data driven by a few common factors
(Section 5).

**5. Experiments.** Three numerical studies:

- a 200-item 0–1 knapsack with $\pm 10\%$ weight uncertainty, where full protection cost
  about 5.5% of the nominal value but a violation bound of about 0.57% cost only about 1.54%;
- a 150-asset portfolio problem, in which raising $\Gamma$ first diversifies the portfolio
  and, past a point, jumps to the single safest asset (Soyster's answer);
- the NETLIB problem PILOT4, where rows have few uncertain coefficients (at most 29), so a
  strong guarantee needs a budget close to full protection and the savings are smaller.

Our own version of the knapsack study is in
[The price of robustness](../budget-of-uncertainty.qmd#the-price-of-robustness-a-knapsack-experiment).

## Why it matters

The budget-of-uncertainty set (often called the *budgeted* or *Γ-uncertainty* set) became
the default uncertainty set in applied robust optimization, largely because of
contribution 2: a modeller can add robustness to an existing LP or MIP without changing the
solver. The same authors carried the idea over to combinatorial problems in
@bertsimas2003, and its link to norm-based uncertainty sets was made precise by
Bertsimas, Pachamanova and Sim [-@bertsimas2004norms]. For a broad view of what followed, see the survey of @bertsimas2011.
